extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific classification, naturalists, philosophers of science, and anyone studying inductive method and taxonomy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for forming natural (scientific) classifications, naming schemes, and arranging groups into series so as to best support inductive inquiry and memory. Includes guidance on choice of characters, the role of types, treatment of anomalies, nomenclature, and arranging kinds by degree of a phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all varieties and affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: “can not determine the group in which any one object can most conveniently be placed, without taking into consideration all the varieties of existing objects, all at least which have any degree of affinity with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning an object to a group, survey the whole range of existing objects that have any degree of affinity; placement must be made with reference to the total set of potentially related things, not by isolated comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing scientific classification on merely simple/perceptible properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial classifications tend to select properties which are simple, easily conceived, and perceptible at first view (e.g., Tournefort’s corolla-shape, Linnæus’s number of stamens and pistils), but these are "seldom much adapted to the ends of that Classification which is the subject of our present remarks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let facility of recognition be the main criterion; trivial obvious characters (even if easy to remember) may be of little scientific interest and can mislead habits of thought away from more informative groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form groups that allow many and important general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ends of scientific classification are best answered, when the objects are formed into groups respecting which a greater number of general propositions can be made, and those propositions more important, than could be made respecting any other groups into which the same things could be distributed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer divisions that maximize the number and importance of general laws or assertions that can be predicated of the members; evaluate candidate groupings by their power to support useful generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal properties or sure marks as classificatory foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The properties, therefore, according to which objects are classified, should, if possible, be those which are causes of many other properties; or, at any rate, which are sure marks of them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, base classification on attributes that are causes (most direct/sure) of many other properties; if cause is inaccessible, choose reliable correlated effects as diagnostic marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: When causes are not diagnostic, select prominent effects as marks
rubrics_metrics.description: “Instead of the cause, we must generally select some of its more prominent effects, which may serve as marks of the other effects and of the cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the underlying causal property cannot be used for diagnosis, choose observable effects that reliably indicate the causal property and thereby the broader class membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Natural (philosophical) over Technical (artificial) classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification is 'Natural' when it corresponds to spontaneous tendencies of the mind by placing together objects most similar in their general aspect; technical/artificial arrangements group by arbitrarily selected circumstances and may juxtapose dissimilar objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor classifications that group items by their general similarity and shared important properties (natural groups); avoid arbitrary criteria that conjoin unrelated things merely by a single selected circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select externally recognizable marks when needed for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Although natural groups may rest on internal structure, practical classification requires some property or set of properties more readily recognizable by the observer (e.g., De Blainville’s reliance on differences in external integuments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the classificatory characters include features that can be practically observed without destroying the specimen, so genus and species can be recognized in the field or routine practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive knowledge of properties is necessary for good classification
rubrics_metrics.description: “how extensive a knowledge of the properties of objects is necessary for making a good classification of them.” Classification and knowledge improve each other: a good classification draws attention to the properties on which it is founded and facilitates discovery of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build classifications on broad empirical knowledge; expect classification to be iterative—improved knowledge refines classification, and good classification points to new properties to investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor classification to the end or purpose in view
rubrics_metrics.description: “The properties...which are here meant by importance? It has reference to the particular end in view; and the same objects, therefore, may admit with propriety of several different classifications.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose those attributes most relevant to the intended use: e.g., farmers classify plants as useful vs weed, geologists by strata; multiple valid classifications may coexist depending on practical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: For general knowledge, prefer attributes that confer marked individuality (natural groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying objects to extend knowledge of all their properties, the most important attributes are those that render things like one another and unlike other things, giving the class 'the most marked individuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general scientific taxonomy, prefer characters that indicate a wide set of common properties (those that 'fill the largest space in their existence') rather than narrow utilitarian distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes are determined by characters, not merely by Type
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Whewell: though classes are often 'suggested by types,' they are not 'determined by a type' alone. 'They are determined by characters, but these are not arbitrary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define classes by enumerating the characters (definitive marks) that indicate common parentage or affinities; use type-specimens only as mental illustrations, not as the exclusive test of membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for anomalies and imperfect diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups frequently include anomalies; artificial 'diagnosis' is imperfect and 'in certain cases this character is made to yield to the general weight of natural affinities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to include exceptions within a class; diagnostic characters may not be universal—treat anomalies as part of the group if overall affinities prevail, and record 'Anomalies' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute classes by all universal characters and most characters admitting exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The class, therefore, is constituted by the possession of all the characters which are universal, and most of those which admit of exceptions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct definitions that require universal characters and the majority of non-universal but characteristic properties; allow membership for specimens that lack one or more non-universal characters if compensated by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek characters that point to numerous indefinite (unknown) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is 'to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diagnostic marks that are good indicators of other (possibly yet-undiscovered) properties, so the classification aids inference and prediction about members' unknown traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify Kinds into series when investigating a particular phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: For study of a particular phenomenon, bring into one class all Kinds exhibiting it and 'arrange those Kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most of it, and terminating with those which exhibit least.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the classificatory goal is to discover laws of a phenomenon, arrange instances by degree of manifestation to facilitate inductive comparison (Concomitant Variations method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Concomitant Variations method for special inductive classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging instances in the order implied in the fourth Method of Experimental Inquiry (Concomitant Variations) is necessary: 'facts which increase or diminish together, and disappear together, are either cause and effect, or effects of a common cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order and compare cases by correlated variations in the phenomenon to infer causal relations; classification by degree is often the only practical way to apply this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt nomenclature that conveys maximal independent significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nomenclature's merit is to 'convey, by the mode of their construction, as much information as possible'—either by formation indicating key properties (ideal) or by indicating natural affinities (binary nomenclature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design names to aid memory and convey distinguishing information: where possible encode key properties in the name; otherwise use hierarchical names (genus + specific epithet) to indicate proximate affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hierarchical/binary (or ternary) nomenclature to economize names
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary nomenclature (genus + species) "immensely economiz[es] the use of names" and prevents an intolerable burden on memory; ternary construction may be used if further extension is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a hierarchical naming system (binary in biology) to keep the total number of distinct names manageable and to encode relational information; expand to ternary constructions if necessary for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: For targeted inductive investigation, choose a type-species displaying the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: When classification is made for the express purpose of a special inductive inquiry, 'it is not optional, but necessary for fulfilling the conditions of a correct Inductive Method, that we should establish a type-species or genus, namely, the one which exhibits in the most eminent degree the particular phenomenon under investigation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an exemplar (type) that best exhibits the phenomenon as a reference point for arranging other kinds and for structuring the inductive inquiry.
